lead: Water in a kettle, LPG in a cylinder, steam entering a turbine: each is a pure fluid whose state is fixed by pressure P, molar volume V and temperature T. Plot every equilibrium state and you get a surface. Its three flat views, P–V, P–T and T–V, are the phase diagrams. They show which phase exists, where two phases coexist, and where boiling stops being possible at all. Every equation of state is drawn on them.
prereq: You need: system, state, intensive and extensive properties and the meaning of a pure substance, from the basic concepts of thermodynamics.

sections.h3: The P-V-T surface and its three views

blocks.text: A pure fluid has one chemical species. In equilibrium its state is fixed by any two of P (pressure, in Pa or bar), T (temperature, in K) and V (molar volume, in m³/mol). The third follows.
Plot all such states with P up, V to the right and T going back. The sheet you get is the P-V-T surface.

Cut the surface three ways. At constant T you get a P–V isotherm. At constant P you get a T–V isobar. At constant V you get a P–T isochore. Each cut is a flat drawing that loses one variable but keeps every phase boundary.

Each view answers a different question. P–V answers work questions, because work is ∫P dV. P–T answers stability questions: which phase exists. T–V answers density questions: how much the volume changes on heating.
For water at 1 bar the two ends of the two-phase region are v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001043 m³/kg (saturated liquid) and v<sub>g</sub> = 1.694 m³/kg (saturated vapour).

A liquid far from the critical point has nearly vertical P–V isotherms, so its volume hardly changes. Two coefficients say how little. The volume expansivity β = (1/V)(∂V/∂T)P measures growth on heating; the isothermal compressibility κ = −(1/V)(∂V/∂P)T measures shrinkage on squeezing. When both are nearly constant, ln(V2/V1) = β(T2 − T1) − κ(P2 − P1). For liquid water at 25 °C, β ≈ 2.6 × 10−4 K−1 and κ ≈ 4.5 × 10−5 bar−1: raising the pressure by 100 bar shrinks it by only about 0.45 %.

Below the critical temperature a P–V isotherm has three parts. The left branch rises almost vertically: liquid hardly compresses. The right branch falls gently: vapour does compress. Between them the isotherm is horizontal at one pressure, the vapour pressure P<sup>sat</sup>(T).

The flat part is the two-phase region. Its left end is saturated liquid, the last liquid before a bubble of vapour appears. Its right end is saturated vapour, the last vapour before a drop of liquid appears. The horizontal length is v<sub>g</sub> − v<sub>f</sub>.

Repeat for every temperature below the critical temperature T<sub>c</sub>. The left ends trace the saturated-liquid curve, the right ends the saturated-vapour curve. Together they close the saturation dome, also called the vapour dome. Inside the dome liquid and vapour coexist at the same P and T but at different V. A mixture of quality x has V = (1 − x)v<sub>f</sub> + x·v<sub>g,</sub> where x is the mass fraction of vapour and v<sub>f</sub> and v<sub>g</sub> are the saturated-liquid and saturated-vapour volumes.

The two curves meet at the critical point: for water, T<sub>c</sub> = 374 °C and P<sub>c</sub> = 221 bar. There saturated liquid and saturated vapour are identical, the latent heat is zero, and the meniscus between them disappears.

sections.h3: The P-T phase diagram and the phase rule

blocks.text: The P–T diagram is the most-used view. Three curves split the plane into solid, liquid and vapour regions. The sublimation curve separates solid from vapour. The fusion curve separates solid from liquid. The vaporisation curve separates liquid from vapour and ends at the critical point. All three meet at the triple point: for water, 0.01 °C and 0.00611 bar, where ice, liquid water and steam coexist.
For water the fusion curve leans left, so ice melts when the pressure rises. That is unusual; for most substances the fusion curve leans right.

Above the critical point the liquid and vapour regions merge. The fluid there is supercritical — neither liquid nor gas. No amount of pressure liquefies it while T stays above T<sub>c</sub>. Supercritical carbon dioxide is used to strip caffeine from coffee beans, and dense supercritical water is studied as a reaction medium.

blocks.where: F is the number of intensive variables you may fix freely (degrees of freedom); C = 1 is the number of components; P<sub>ph</sub> is the number of phases present. P on its own always means pressure, in bar or Pa.

blocks.text: One phase gives F = 2: choose T and P independently. Two phases give F = 1: choosing T fixes P = P<sup>sat</sup>(T). Three phases give F = 0: the triple point is one single state.

sections.h3: Mathematical representation: the equation of state

blocks.text: An equation of state is an algebraic relation among P, V and T for a fluid: f(P, V, T) = 0, or P = f(V, T). Every curve in the diagrams above is a solution of it. Some syllabi call this whole topic volumetric properties of pure fluids.
The simplest relation is the ideal gas law, PV = RT, where R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) is the gas constant. It holds when molecules are far apart; the next chapter develops it.

Real fluids need corrections. The compressibility factor Z = PV/RT measures the departure from ideal behaviour: Z = 1 for an ideal gas, Z < 1 when attraction between molecules pulls them together, and Z > 1 when their own size pushes them apart (high pressure). Virial equations add terms in 1/V. Cubic equations such as van der Waals carry two constants, a for attraction and b for molecular size, and can reproduce the dome and the critical point — see virial and cubic equations and compressibility factor.

An equation of state can also be built from the forces between pairs of molecules, but that is statistical mechanics, not this course. Mixtures, fugacity and the Clapeyron equation come later, with solution thermodynamics and property relations.

spec.aria: Pressure on a log scale from 0.0001 to 1000 bar against temperature from minus 60 to 420 degrees Celsius. The sublimation curve rises to the triple point at 0.01 degrees and 0.00611 bar; from there the vaporisation curve rises to the critical point at 374 degrees and 221 bar, and the nearly vertical fusion line leans slightly left. A dashed line at 1 bar carries three marked states: 25 degrees liquid, 99.6 degrees boiling and 120 degrees vapour.

examples.question: Water is held at 1 bar (100 kPa). (a) Name the phase at 25 °C, at 99.6 °C and at 120 °C. (b) Treat the vapour at 120 °C and 1 bar as ideal and estimate its specific volume. Data: R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), M = 18.015 g/mol.
steps: At 1 bar the saturation temperature of water is 99.6 °C. The normal boiling point, 100.0 °C, is defined at 1 atm = 1.01325 bar, slightly above 1 bar.
25 °C is below the saturation temperature. The fluid is a compressed (subcooled) liquid. One phase, so F = 3 − 1 = 2.
99.6 °C is the saturation temperature. Liquid and vapour coexist; any quality 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 is possible. Two phases, F = 1, so P alone fixes T.
120 °C is above the saturation temperature. The fluid is superheated vapour. One phase, F = 2.
On the P–T diagram (figure above) the 1 bar line crosses the vaporisation curve once, at 99.6 °C: below it is liquid, above it vapour.
Specific gas constant: R<sub>s</sub> = R/M = 8.314/0.018015 = 461.5 J/(kg·K).
Ideal gas law per unit mass: v = R<sub>s</sub>·T/P = 461.5 × 393.15/100 000 = 1.8144 m³/kg.
Compare with the molar form: V = RT/P = 8.314 × 393.15/100 000 = 0.03269 m³/mol, and 0.03269 m³/mol ÷ 0.018015 kg/mol = 1.8144 m³/kg. Both routes agree.
examples.answer: Liquid at 25 °C, liquid–vapour at 99.6 °C and vapour at 120 °C; the ideal-gas specific volume at 120 °C and 1 bar is 1.8144 m³/kg.

traps: Reading the saturation curve as a single phase. On a P–T diagram every point of the vaporisation curve is a two-phase state: saturated liquid and saturated vapour together. On a P–V diagram the two branches of the dome are saturated liquid and saturated vapour, and only points strictly inside the dome are two-phase mixtures.
Calling the critical point a boiling point. At the critical point liquid and vapour are one phase and the latent heat is zero.
Thinking a gas above T<sub>c</sub> can be liquefied by pressure alone. It cannot; you must first cool it below T<sub>c</sub>.
Putting °C into PV = RT or any ideal-gas formula. Always convert to K.
Mixing molar or specific volume with total volume. V<sub>total</sub> = n·V; phase diagrams use volume per mole or per kilogram.

quiz.q: Define the triple point and give its value for water.
quiz.a: The single pressure and temperature at which solid, liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium. For water: 0.01 °C and 0.00611 bar. F = 0 there.

quiz.q: Write the phase rule for a one-component system and give F for one, two and three phases.
quiz.a: F = C − P<sub>ph</sub> + 2 = 3 − P<sub>ph,</sub> where P<sub>ph</sub> is the number of phases present. One phase F = 2, two phases F = 1, three phases F = 0.

quiz.q: Why is part of a P–V isotherm horizontal below T<sub>c</sub>?
quiz.a: Because liquid and vapour coexist there. At a fixed T the saturation pressure is fixed, so P stays constant while V runs from v<sub>f</sub> to v<sub>g</sub>.

quiz.q: A sample of water is at 1 bar and 150 °C. How many degrees of freedom does it have, and what phase is it?
quiz.a: 150 °C is above the saturation temperature at 1 bar, which is 99.6 °C, so the water is superheated vapour. One phase present, so F = 3 − 1 = 2: for a single phase of a pure fluid, T and P can be chosen independently.

quiz.q: Water at 250 bar is cooled from 400 °C to 100 °C. Does it boil? Explain using the phase diagram.
quiz.a: No. 250 bar lies above P<sub>c</sub> = 221 bar, so the constant-pressure path never crosses the vaporisation curve. Liquid and vapour never coexist: the fluid passes continuously from supercritical to a dense liquid, with no horizontal segment and no latent heat.

beyond: Not for the exam. Plant design uses equations of state fitted to measured saturation pressures and densities, and reference formulations such as IAPWS-95 for water. Supercritical CO₂ power cycles and CO₂ pipelines operate where the dome flattens near the critical point. Search next for IAPWS-95 and critical point universality.
